---
title: "Get started with powerape in Stata"
description: >
  Install the command, run a first power analysis for an average partial
  effect, and read its output: the six steps of the R article, in the same
  world.
---

```{r helpers, include = FALSE}
root <- normalizePath(getwd(), winslash = "/")
while (!file.exists(file.path(root, "DESCRIPTION")) && dirname(root) != root)
  root <- dirname(root)
source(file.path(root, "precompute", "helpers.R"))
st   <- stata_results("getting-started")
secs <- stata_seconds("getting-started")
```

In a probit or logit model the coefficient is not the quantity anyone
interprets. Conclusions are stated in probability points: the treatment
raises take-up by ten percentage points. That quantity is the **average
partial effect (APE)**, and it depends on all coefficients and on the
covariate distribution, so power tools that work in coefficient units cannot
say how many observations are needed to detect it. `powerape` states the
effect in APE units and simulates the whole study: it draws covariates and
outcomes, fits the model, computes the APE with a delta-method confidence
interval, and checks a **claim** on that interval (Riesthuis, 2024):

* `minimum`: the lower bound of the interval exceeds the smallest effect size
  of interest (SESOI), so the effect is meaningfully large. This is the
  default claim.
* `detect`: the interval excludes zero.
* `equivalence`: the interval lies inside (−SESOI, +SESOI), so the effect is
  too small to matter.

The Stata command `powerape` is a port of the R package of the same name and
is documented side by side with it on this site. This page takes the six
steps of the R article [Powering the minimum-effect claim](minimum-effect.html)
through Stata, in the same world, and then shows what is specific to Stata:
who fits the simulated studies, and how to start from pilot data.

## Installation

<div class="wrap-code">

```stata
net install powerape, from("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jespernwulff/powerape-stata/main/")
mata: mata mlib index
powerape version
```

</div>

`net install` copies the command, its help file and its Mata library;
`mata: mata mlib index` makes the new library known to the running Stata
session (needed once, right after installing); `powerape version` checks
that the command and the library belong together. To update, add `replace`
to `net install`. `net get powerape, from(...)` with the same address copies
two files into the current folder: `showcase.do`, a guided tour of every
subcommand, and `build.do`, which recompiles the Mata library.

Stata 16 or later is required. The control-function route for endogenous
treatments uses `cfprobit` (Stata 18 or later), and computing interaction
effects with `ginteff` itself, an option, needs that command from the Stata
Journal (`net install st0711, from(http://www.stata-journal.com/software/sj23-2)`).
The command has been tested on StataNow 19.5. After installation,
`help powerape` opens the help file, which is also
[on this site](stata-help.html).

## Step 1: describe the world

One command describes the data-generating process (DGP) the study will
sample from and stores it under a name, the way `estimates store` stores
results. Here: a probit model, a binary treatment given to half the sample,
two covariates, an outcome rate of 0.30 without treatment, and covariates
that explain 15% of the latent variation.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
stata_show("getting-started", "world")
```

Each variable is written as `(name, type options)`: `binary p()` or `normal
mean() sd()`. The nuisance side is set on two friendly scales, the
**baseline outcome rate** (`baseline()`) and the covariates' **latent
pseudo-R²** (`signal()`), and `powerape` solves for the coefficients that
produce them. `correlation()` sets the latent correlation among the focal
variable and the covariates. A pilot data set or a fitted pilot model can
take the place of these guesses; see [Pilot data](#pilot-data) below.

## Step 2: pin the true APE

Suppose prior evidence suggests a true effect of ten percentage points, and
effects below five points would not justify the program: the planning value
is 0.10 and the SESOI is 0.05.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
stata_show("getting-started", "pin")
```

`powerape setape` solves for the coefficient of the treatment that makes the
true APE exactly 0.10, given everything else, and refuses with an
explanation when the target cannot exist (an APE of +0.40 at a baseline rate
of 0.85, say). For interaction designs `powerape setaie` pins the average
interaction effect instead; see [Interaction effects](interaction-effects.html).

## Step 3: power for the claim

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
stata_show("getting-started", "power")
```

In each of the `r num(st["power", "nsim"], 0)` replications `powerape` drew
a sample of `r num(st["power", "n"], 0)` observations, fitted it, and asked
whether the 90 percent confidence interval of the APE lies above the SESOI
(a one-sided test at the 5 percent level). It did in
`r num(100 * st["power", "power"], 1)` percent of them. The line beginning
`fit:` says who fitted the simulated studies: Stata's own `probit`, with the
APE and its standard error computed from `e(b)` and `e(V)` exactly as
`margins` computes them.

Read the **outcome distribution**, not only the power. About a third of the
studies would show an effect different from zero but could not claim that it
clears the SESOI ("detect-only"): exactly the inconclusive result that a
power analysis for detection alone hides. The R article finds the same split
in the same world, up to simulation error.

### Stored results

Every subcommand stores its results in `r()`.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
stata_show("getting-started", "stored")
```

Results also stay available by name: `powerape list` shows the stored DGPs
and results, and the option `name()` keeps a result under a name of your
choice (see [Justified alpha](justified-alpha.html) for a use).

## Step 4: required sample size and the power curve

`powerape n` searches for the sample size that reaches the target power, then
confirms it with a high-precision run and moves it upward, never down, if the
confirmation falls short.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
stata_show("getting-started", "n")
```

A search runs thousands of simulated studies (here the confirmation stage
alone ran 2,000), so this call uses the Mata engine, `engine(mata)`, a
self-contained port of the R package's fitting routine that is many times
faster than calling `probit`. [Engines](#engines-who-fits-the-simulated-studies)
below explains the choice. The search took
`r num(secs[["n"]], 0)` seconds.

A power curve evaluates a list of sample sizes on the same footing.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
stata_show("getting-started", "curve")
```

`r(results)` holds the curve as a matrix, ready to plot:

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
stata_show("getting-started", "curve-plot", output = FALSE)
stata_figure("getting-started-curve.svg",
             alt = "Power of the minimum-effect claim at sample sizes from 500 to 3,000, rising from about 0.3 to about 0.9 and crossing 0.8 near 2,100.",
             caption = "Power of the minimum-effect claim against the sample size, with the 80 percent target.")
```

## When n is fixed: the minimum detectable effect

Often the sample is given: the archive has the firms it has. `powerape mde`
turns the question around and finds the smallest true APE that the claim
reaches with 80 percent power, with the same confirmation stage as
`powerape n`.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
stata_show("getting-started", "mde")
```

With `r num(st["mde", "n"], 0)` observations, the study can show an effect
to be meaningfully above 0.05 if the true effect is about
`r num(st["mde", "mde"], 3)` or larger.

## Step 5: how fragile is this to the contextual guesses?

The baseline rate and the covariate signal are guesses. `powerape robust`
repeats the analysis over a grid of them and reports the worst case (Hancock
& Feng, 2026). By default the APE is re-pinned in every scenario
(`pin(ape)`), so only the precision of the estimate varies.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
stata_show("getting-started", "robust")
```

Dropping `nonmax` adds **n_max**, the largest required sample size across
the scenarios, at 90 percent power by default (`nmaxpower()`): the sample
size that insures the design against the guesses. `mode(mde)` reports the
minimum detectable effect per scenario instead of power.

## Step 6: the citable paragraph

`powerape statement` writes the last result as a methods paragraph for a
grant application or a preregistration.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
stata_show("getting-started", "statement")
```

## Engines: who fits the simulated studies

The simulation draws the data in Mata. Fitting each simulated study can be
left to Stata or done in Mata:

* `engine(stata)`, the default, writes every simulated study to a temporary
  frame and fits it with Stata's own `probit` or `logit`, with
  `vce(cluster)` for panels and `cfprobit` for endogenous treatments. The
  effects are computed from `e(b)` and `e(V)` by the closed-form delta
  method that `margins` uses.
* `engine(mata)` fits each study with a Mata port of the R package's
  routine (Fisher scoring, expected information).

On the same seed both engines draw the same studies, so they can be compared
directly:

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
stata_show("getting-started", "engine-mata")
```

The power is the same, `r num(st["engine_mata", "power"], 3)`. The outcome
split differs by one study of `r num(st["engine_mata", "nsim"], 0)`, because
`probit` computes standard errors from the observed information and the Mata
engine from the expected information, which moves an interval that sits
right at a boundary. The Mata engine took
`r num(secs[["engine_mata"]], 1)` seconds, `probit`
`r num(secs[["power"]], 1)`. Use the Mata engine for searches, curves and
sweeps, and confirm the final design with Stata's estimator.

`effects(margins)` goes one step further and computes every APE with
`margins` itself (or with `ginteff` for interaction effects). On the same
seed it reproduces the closed-form results exactly:

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
stata_show("getting-started", c("effects-closed", "effects-margins"))
```

It is also slower (`r num(secs[["effects_margins"]], 1)` against
`r num(secs[["effects_closed"]], 1)` seconds for these 100 replications), so
its use is as a check. `engine()` and `effects()` given on one command apply
to that command only; `powerape engine` shows and sets the defaults for the
session:

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
stata_show("getting-started", "session")
```

## Pilot data

When pilot data are available, the covariates can come from them instead of
from parametric guesses. Here is a small simulated pilot:

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
stata_show("getting-started", "pilot-data", output = FALSE)
```

`empirical` resamples whole rows of the pilot data in memory and calibrates
the outcome model to the stated baseline rate and signal. A listed focal
variable is resampled jointly with the covariates; one specified as
`(name, binary p())` is drawn independently of them instead.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
stata_show("getting-started", "pilot-empirical")
```

`fromfit` takes the world from a fitted `probit` or `logit` model: the
nuisance coefficients and the pilot rows come from the fit, and `setape`
re-solves the focal coefficient for the planning value. `baseline()` can
override the pilot's outcome rate.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
stata_show("getting-started", "pilot-fromfit")
```

The R functions for the two routes are `ape_dgp_empirical()` and
`ape_dgp_from_fit()`. Panel data and endogenous treatments have their own
routes, `panel` and `iv`; see [Panel designs](panel-designs.html) and
[IV designs](iv-designs.html).
